prompt: Some people believe that employees should be allowed to work from home instead of going to an office every day. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
essay:
I used to think working from home was mainly for IT workers, but now many companies offer it to ordinary office staff. In my view, employees should be allowed to work remotely several days a week, although keeping some days in the office is still necessary.

The first benefit is time. When I worked in an office in Astana, I was spending almost two hours on road every day. Last year our team has started working at home twice a week, and I could finally have breakfast with my family. This extra time also helped me to finish tasks without feeling exhausted. A company can benefit too because it does not need so much space for desks.

Another advantage is concentration. At home, people can choose a quiet room, and they are not interrupted for every small question. However, it depends from living conditions. Someone who share one room with children probably works better in an office. Employers should not assume that all workers have same situation.

There are disadvantages as well. New employees sometimes need guidance and if they only send messages, misunderstanding can continue for days, the manager may not notice until deadline. I have seen this when a new colleague didn't understood the instructions and nobody checked his progress. Regular meetings in person would make such problems less serious.

For these reasons, I support a mixed system. Let people choose home days for individual work, but bring teams together for training and decisions that needs discussion. Remote work is useful, provided companies manage it with clear rules.

They enter workplace with theoretical confidence and very little experience of deadlines, safety procedures or working with clients. If departments build partnerships with local firms, students could complete projects that resemble the work they will actually do. Such exposure helps them to make an informed career choice and compete on labour market. It also saves employers from spending months on basic training.

There is also the issue of unequal opportunity. Students from wealthy families can arrange unpaid placements through personal contacts. Others cannot afford this route, and it is difficult for them to receive the same experiences. Others argue that universities should pursue knowledge for its own sake. They say subjects like philosophy and pure mathematics deserve attention even without an immediate job benefit. This is reasonable, but I see it as secondary.

Overall, I would put employability at the centre of university programmes. Academic knowledge still matters because it provides a foundation for future learning, but students need chances to apply it while studying.

prompt: Air pollution is becoming a serious problem in many cities around the world. What are the main causes of this problem, and what measures can governments and individuals take to reduce it?
essay:
In many large cities, air pollution is no longer something people notice only on the news. On cold mornings in Almaty, the mountains sometimes disappear behind a grey layer. The problem has several causes, and both public authorities and residents have ways to reduce it.

First, road traffic contributes to dirty air. Older cars release more harmful gases, especially when engines are left running in queues. People living near busy roads are exposed for many hours, which make children especially vulnerable. Also, public transport may be unreliable in outer districts. This makes it worse. People choose their cars even for short journeys.

Second, heating systems are another source. Some buildings still use coal, and emissions become trapped when there is little wind. Also, small factories may be located near housing, and checks on them can be infrequent. It is the same issue. As a result, health problems are difficult to avoid.

There are practical solutions. First, local governments should create bus lanes and improve the frequency of services. If a bus arrives every ten minutes, commuters may leave their cars at home. prompt: Some people believe that testing new medicines on animals is necessary to protect human health, while others argue that animal testing should be completely banned. To what extent do you agree or disagree with banning animal testing?
essay:
Before a new medicine reaches patients, researchers need evidence that it will not cause serious harm. Animal testing is one method for collecting this evidence, although it raises important concerns. I do not support a complete ban, but I think its use should be tightly limited.

The main argument against a ban is patient safety. A treatment that appears safe in a computer model may behave differently in a living body. For example, scientists may need to observe whether a new drug damages organs over several weeks, not only whether it kills particular cells in a laboratory. If companies would skip every animal study, some risks might be discovered only after volunteers take the medicine. This would be a serious problem, especially for patients which are already ill.

A second issue is the speed of medical research. Some illnesses have few effective treatments. When a laboratory has found a promising substance, the researchers needs a clear path to test it before human trials. Without this information, doctors could be difficult to judge its risks. Removing one step without a reliable replacement could make the process slower. However, this does not mean that every experiment is justified or that cost should be the only consideration.

There are strong reasons to reduce animal tests. Animals can suffer, and results from their bodies do not always apply to humans. Governments should require researchers to explain why other methods cannot answer a question, and to use the smallest number of animals possible. Laboratories must also be responsible of the conditions in which animals are kept. Independent inspections are needed, otherwise the rules may exist only on paper.

In short, I disagree with a total prohibition. The priority should be protecting people while improving other testing methods, so that animal experiments can gradually become less necessary.

prompt: Some people believe that governments should invest more money in space exploration, while others argue that this money should be spent on solving problems on Earth. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

Governments face difficult choices when deciding how to distribute public funds. Space exploration attracts considerable investment, yet many communities still struggle with inadequate healthcare and basic infrastructure. I believe space research deserves continued support, provided it does not take priority over essential public services.

Supporters of space programmes argue that their benefits extend far beyond scientific curiosity. Satellites help meteorologists predict severe weather and allow farmers to monitor changes in soil conditions. Such information can prevent significant economic losses. Researchers, many of whom working across borders, also develop technologies that eventually become useful in other industries. Although these benefits are difficult to calculate precisely, but they should not be dismissed. Furthermore, international space projects can encourage cooperation between countries that have political disagreements on Earth.

Those who oppose large investments in space research raise an equally important concern. In developing countries, hospitals often lack equipment, while rural schools struggle to recruit qualified teachers. A mission that fails can absorb resources which could otherwise improve these services. Moreover, scientific discoveries do not necessarily produce immediate practical benefits. Some projects require enormous expenditure, even though the results may remain uncertain for decades. If governments would publish independent evaluations of major missions, taxpayers could better understand whether such spending is justified.

In my opinion, the two priorities should not be treated as completely incompatible. Governments could establish a limited but stable research budget while directing a larger proportion of public spending towards urgent social needs. International partnerships could also distribute the financial burden among participating nations.

Ultimately, exploring space is a worthwhile ambition, but its value should be considered alongside conditions on Earth. Responsible investment requires both scientific ambition and attention to people's immediate needs.

prompt: Some people believe that longer prison sentences are the most effective way to reduce crime. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
essay:
Longer prison sentences are often presented as a straightforward response to rising crime. Although serious offenders sometimes need to be separated from society for many years, I disagree that increasing the length of imprisonment is the most effective general solution.

The first problem is that punishment does not necessarily change the reasons why someone committed a crime. A person who steals because of unemployment may leave prison facing exactly the same difficulties. If the experience has not helped them develop useful skills, they may return to illegal activities. This is why rehabilitation should receive more attention. Education and job training can give prisoners an opportunity to make different decisions after their release.

Another consideration is prevention. Governments could direct more resources towards young people who are at risk of becoming involved in crime. For example, schools might provide additional counselling and activities after lessons. These measures would not eliminate every offence, but they could help some teenagers avoid harmful choices. Preventing crime seems a more reliable answer for crime than simply increasing punishment after damage has already occurred.

Nevertheless, prisons still have an important function. Violent offenders may present a continuing threat, and the public deserves protection. Longer sentences can also demonstrate that certain actions have serious consequences. This argument is reasonable, although it does not prove that longer sentences are effective in every situation.

I therefore favour an approach that combines suitable punishment with practical rehabilitation and early intervention. The justice system should aim not only to punish offenders but also to prevent them from returning back to crime. Such an approach may gradually build trust towards the courts and make communities safer.

prompt: In many countries, the proportion of elderly people is increasing as people live longer and fewer children are born. What problems can an aging population create for society, and what benefits can it bring?

Living longer is one of the most significant achievements of modern healthcare. Yet when the proportion of older citizens rises, societies must reconsider how they organize employment, healthcare and support for families. An aging population creates financial and practical challenges, but it also offers benefits that are often overlooked.

One major difficulty is the growing demand for healthcare and pensions. Older people are more likely to need regular medical treatment, particularly when they live with several long-term conditions. This puts a pressure on public budgets, especially in countries where a relatively small working population supports a large number of pensioners. Families may also be affected. An adult who cares for an elderly parent might reduce their working hours or leave employment temporarily. Flexible retirement arrangements would allow capable older workers to remain employed without forcing everyone to work longer. prompt: Climate change is becoming one of the most serious challenges facing the world. What are the main human causes of climate change, and what measures should governments and individuals take to address it?

Climate change is driven largely by decisions about how societies produce energy, manufacture goods and use land. Although individuals contribute to emissions through everyday consumption, the largest sources are connected to infrastructure and industrial systems. Effective action therefore requires changes at both national and personal levels.

Burning fossil fuels remains a central cause because electricity generation, heating and transport release substantial quantities of greenhouse gases. In countries where coal is still widely used, replacing power stations cannot happen immediately, since electricity must remain reliable and affordable. Governments should invest in renewable capacity while improving transmission networks and energy storage, rather than announcing targets without preparing the infrastructure required to meet them. Buildings also account for considerable energy consumption. Insulation programmes could reduce heating demand, particularly in regions with severe winters, and would lower household costs over time. Such investments should be accompanied with clear efficiency standards for new construction. There is also agriculture and deforestation. When forests are cleared, stored carbon is released and fewer trees remain to absorb future emissions. Protecting existing forests is often less expensive than attempting to restore damaged ecosystems decades later. Governments could make agricultural subsidies conditional on sustainable land management, although this would require careful monitoring. Industrial emissions present another difficulty. Steel and cement production cannot be fully decarbonised simply by encouraging citizens to recycle more. Public investment in cleaner production methods and predictable carbon regulations could give manufacturers a reason to modernise their facilities.

Individual behaviour still matters. People can reduce unnecessary car journeys, choose durable products and improve energy efficiency at home. Yet these choices depend on available alternatives. Asking households to abandon cars is unrealistic when public transport is unreliable. Similarly, environmentally friendly appliances may remain unaffordable without financial assistance. Policies should therefore make lower-carbon choices convenient rather than relying entirely on personal guilt.

prompt: Some people believe that artificial intelligence will improve working life, while others are concerned that it will replace many jobs and create new problems for employees. To what extent do you agree that the increasing use of artificial intelligence in workplaces is a positive development?
essay:
Whether artificial intelligence improves working life depends less on the technology itself than on the decisions made by employers. Automation can remove repetitive tasks and support better judgement, but it can also increase insecurity when workers have little influence over how it is introduced. I consider AI a positive development overall, provided its benefits are shared and employees retain meaningful control over important decisions.

One advantage is that software can reduce the time professionals spend on routine administration. In healthcare, for instance, an AI system might organise patient records or highlight unusual test results, leaving doctors more time for direct care. This does not mean the software should make final diagnoses. Rather, it can help specialists concentrate on decisions requiring experience and responsibility. Similar improvements are possible in engineering, where automated checks may identify defects before they become expensive failures. If employers would use these savings to improve training and reduce excessive workloads, the benefits could extend beyond productivity figures.

The main risk is not simply that certain tasks will disappear. It is that the transition may happen faster than employees can adapt. An experienced administrator whose duties are automated cannot necessarily move into data analysis after a short online course. Retraining needs time, financial support and a realistic understanding of the opportunities available. There is little value in promising new careers if the training begins only after workers have lost their income.

Accountability creates another concern. When automated systems influence recruitment or performance reviews, employees should be able to question their conclusions. Companies need a policy under which staff can challenge decisions that they were made by software. Such safeguards are particularly important in workplaces where employees have limited bargaining power.

Ultimately, AI should be judged by more than the number of tasks it performs. In a long term, its success will depend on whether productivity gains translate into better jobs, fairer opportunities and decisions that people can understand and contest.

prompt: Some people believe that traditional customs should be preserved in their original form, while others argue that traditions need to change as society develops. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
essay:
Customs change as people move, marry and live differently from their grandparents. Some argue that traditions must be protected in their original form; others believe they should evolve. I favour preservation of their meaning rather than every detail.

There are good reasons to keep familiar rituals. At Nauryz, for example, preparing food together and visiting older relatives give younger people a sense of belonging that an ordinary day rarely provides. The value is not simply the dishes or clothing. It is the time spent together. When children learn the stories behind a ceremony which origins are centuries old, they can connect family memories with a wider history. Traditional festivals can also attract tourists and bring money to local businesses.

Nevertheless, insisting that every practice remain unchanged can make traditions less welcoming. A celebration designed around an extended family may be difficult for someone living alone or far from home. Younger adults may feel attached with the spirit of a custom while being uncomfortable with expectations about gender or marriage. Treating such concerns as disrespect can turn a shared tradition into a obligation. Communities are more likely to keep customs alive when participation is voluntary and people understand why they matter.

The difficulty is deciding what deserves protection. Museums and schools can preserve songs, crafts and oral histories, while families adapt the ways they celebrate. Families can continue sharing meals while allowing younger relatives decide how they participate. If a particular ritual excludes some members of a community, there is little reason to insist on it unchanged.

Traditions survive because people continue to find value in them, not because every generation repeats exactly the same actions. Respect for the past and room for change can exist together.

prompt: Some people believe that maintaining a healthy lifestyle is entirely an individual's responsibility, while others think governments should take a more active role in helping people stay healthy. To what extent do you agree or disagree that health is primarily a personal responsibility?
essay:
A healthy lifestyle is often presented as a matter of personal discipline: eat sensibly, exercise regularly and get enough sleep. Health is not a purely private responsibility. Governments shape many of the conditions in which those choices are made.

To begin with, people cannot follow advice that is unrealistic for their circumstances. Someone working irregular shifts may have little time to cook, while a family living far from a supermarket may rely on convenient, less nutritious food. Telling them to show more willpower overlooks these barriers. Public transport, safe walking routes and affordable sports facilities can make a healthier routine of life easier to maintain. Such measures benefit people who would otherwise struggle to act on medical advice.

Education also has a role. Schools can help children understand nutrition without turning meals into a source of anxiety. Local clinics could offer practical guidance before minor problems become serious, particularly for families which access to healthcare is limited. Such advice should be based in credible evidence. There is also an evidence that early habits are difficult to change, which makes prevention especially valuable.

Personal responsibility remains essential. Governments cannot decide what people eat each evening or whether they go for a walk. Individuals have to take responsibility for their daily routines, and no policy can replace that effort. Yet expecting everyone to make healthy decisions while ignoring unequal access to resources is not a fair approach.

A sensible policy would combine reliable information with practical support. Employers could allow predictable breaks, councils could maintain parks, and schools could provide balanced meals. These steps do not guarantee good health, but they give more people a genuine chance to build healthy decisions rather than leaving prevention to those who can afford it.

prompt: Increasing numbers of people are choosing to live and work in countries other than their own. What are the main advantages and disadvantages of living abroad?
essay:
Moving abroad can transform an ordinary career decision into a much broader personal experience. People leave their home countries for work, study or family reasons, and the outcomes are rarely entirely positive or negative.

The most obvious benefit is exposure to unfamiliar ways of living. A person who studies in another country must learn to navigate institutions, communicate across cultural differences and solve problems without their usual support network. Those skills can be valuable long after they return home. Working overseas may also broaden professional expectations. An engineer who joins an international team, for instance, may discover different approaches to safety or project management and bring them into a later job.

Living among people whose assumptions differ from one's own can challenge comfortable opinions. This does not mean every newcomer becomes open-minded, but everyday encounters can make cultural differences less abstract. Even small experiences, such as being invited to a neighbour's family meal, may change how someone understands belonging.

Housing can be expensive, familiar qualifications may not be recognised, and the sense of being an outsider can persist even for those fluent with the local language. People sometimes become dependent of colleagues for tasks they once managed alone. Meanwhile, the network of friends they left behind remains a source of emotional support, yet time zones and changing routines make those friendships harder to maintain. Moving overseas can carry a emotional cost that is difficult to predict.

For families, whose children have started attending school in a new language, the decision may be particularly complicated. Children often adapt quickly, while their parents struggle with paperwork or employment.

Living abroad can offer considerable growth and opportunity, but it is not a universal shortcut to a better life. Its value depends on the reasons for moving, the support available and the sacrifices a person is prepared to make.

prompt: Homelessness is a growing problem in many cities, including in countries with relatively strong economies. What are the main causes of homelessness, and what measures could governments take to reduce it?
essay:
Homelessness is often discussed as though it results from a single poor decision. In reality, people may lose stable housing after a sequence of events: a rent increase, reduced working hours, an illness or the breakdown of a relationship. Effective policy must address both the shortage of affordable homes and the circumstances that make some households especially vulnerable.

The first priority is prevention. In cities where rents rise faster than wages, even employed tenants can fall behind after one unexpected expense. Short-term rental assistance and access to legal advice could stop a late payment from turning to an eviction. These services should be available before a household reaches a crisis point, not only once its possessions are on the pavement. Local authorities could also monitor eviction filings to identify neighbourhoods where intervention is most urgently needed.

For people already sleeping rough, temporary shelters provide immediate safety but rarely offer a continuous solution to homelessness. A housing-first approach offers stable accommodation before requiring people to resolve every other difficulty in their lives. Once someone has an address, it becomes easier to attend medical appointments, secure employment and maintain contact with support workers. This approach requires a sufficient supply of homes, however; placing people on an endless waiting list is not a solution.

Support must also be tailored. A person escaping domestic violence may need confidential accommodation, while someone recovering from serious illness may need coordinated medical and social care. Such services are more effective when housing teams share responsibility with healthcare providers, without making treatment a condition of keeping a home. Cities should collect a reliable data on outcomes, including whether residents remain housed after a year.

These measures require public investment, but repeated emergency interventions are costly too. A policy that prevents avoidable evictions and gives people stable housing addresses homelessness more directly than one that merely moves them out of sight.

prompt: Some people believe that museums and historic buildings should be modernised to attract more tourists, while others think preserving their original character is more important. To what extent do you agree or disagree that preservation should take priority over attracting visitors?
essay:
A museum can be crowded with visitors and still fail to explain why its collection matters. Historic buildings face a similar problem: modern attractions may bring in revenue while slowly erasing the features that made a place worth visiting. I believe preservation should take priority, although heritage institutions must remain accessible and financially viable.

Original materials carry information that replicas cannot always reproduce. Worn steps, repairs in an old wall and objects altered through everyday use reveal how earlier generations actually lived. Once these details are replaced to create a more attractive setting, the loss is often irreversible. A historic house that looks newly built may impress visitors, but it can also give them a misleading picture of the past. Conservation is therefore not simply a matter of keeping an attractive façade.

Accessibility, on the other hand, need not threaten authenticity. A museum which collection includes traditional textiles can use audio guides, contemporary interviews and thoughtful lighting to make the objects meaningful without altering them. Visitors should be able to understand who made an artefact, how it was used and why it survived.

There are practical limits. Maintaining a fragile building is expensive, and tourism can provide funds that public budgets cannot. But revenue should support conservation priorities, not define them. A proposed renovation ought to be assessed in relation with the site's character, especially when it involves removing original features. If changes are necessary for safety or disability access, curators should explain these decisions for visitors. The compromises then become part of the institution's public responsibility rather than something to conceal.

The best museums do more than protect objects from damage. They preserve context, invite questions and allow visitors to encounter a past that may be unfamiliar or uncomfortable. When financial decisions follow that purpose, attracting tourists and protecting heritage can reinforce one another rather than compete.

prompt: Automation is increasingly replacing tasks previously performed by human workers. Some people believe that this development brings more benefits than disadvantages to society. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
essay:
Automation is becoming part of ordinary workplaces, from warehouses to local banks. I agree that it can bring more benefits than harm, but only if companies take the disruption seriously instead of assuming that new jobs will automatically appear.

In a warehouse, scanning equipment can locate parcels faster than workers checking long printed lists. A manager who used to spend hours correcting these records can now deal with damaged deliveries and customer complaints. Such changes may sound small, but they reduce mistakes that affect hundreds of orders. Automation has also developed on a rapid pace in food production, where machines can handle repetitive work that causes injuries.

The difficulty is what happens to employees whose tasks disappear. A forty-year-old cashier cannot necessarily become a technician after a weekend course. Training programmes are often mentioned in company announcements, yet the information about who will pay for them are missing. Without paid training time, workers with families may be unable to participate. Even experienced staff cannot move in a new role overnight. The problem is even greater in smaller towns where one factory provides much of the employment.

There is another concern about monitoring. Software can measure how quickly employees finish tasks, but a number on a dashboard does not explain why a particular worker was slower. Last year, a friend told me that his company had introduced automatic performance reports, and staff were blamed for delays caused by broken equipment. Managers later adjusted the system. This example shows why workers should be able to question automated judgments.

I still regard automation as an improvement. Businesses gain efficiency, and employees may be released from dull or dangerous duties. But a responsible employer must make a decision whether to retrain people before removing their positions. The technology should serve the workplace, rather than making the workplace fit whatever a machine can measure.

prompt: Many people choose to spend some of their free time doing unpaid voluntary work. Why do people decide to volunteer, and what benefits can volunteering bring to individuals and their communities?
essay:
A few hours of unpaid work may seem insignificant, yet community projects often depend on people who offer exactly that. Volunteering appeals to different age groups for different reasons, and its value extends beyond the immediate help provided.

For students, it offers experience that formal education cannot always supply. Organising a charity event means contacting strangers, handling unexpected problems and making decisions with limited resources. These are useful skills when applying for a first job. Others volunteer because they have experienced a difficulty themselves. A parent whose child received support in hospital may later join a fundraising group, hoping to give other families the same reassurance.

The community gains more than additional labour. In neighbourhoods where elderly residents rarely meet their neighbours, volunteer visitors can reduce isolation and notice when someone needs professional assistance. Environmental groups may also bring residents together to clean a river or improve a neglected park. Their work improves public spaces, but it also creates contacts between people who otherwise would never speak.

These benefits are not automatic. Charities need to explain tasks clearly, give access for training and provide suitable supervision; otherwise volunteers may feel that their time has been wasted. During a local collection last winter, the organisers had promised clear instructions, but on arrival several people were sent between different locations with no explanation. Some did not return. The experience illustrates why good intentions are not enough for organising a useful project.

Local councils can help by offering meeting spaces and publicising opportunities for residents interested on helping, while employers could give staff a few hours for community service. More importantly, organisers should welcome people with limited time rather than expecting a regular commitment from everyone. Small contributions are easier to sustain when volunteers feel respect for their circumstances.

Volunteering benefits the wider community and the individuals involved, but the quality of organisation determines whether enthusiasm becomes lasting help.
